title: Two Fossil Fuel Companies Are Betting Big on Data Centers
gist: Oil and gas infrastructure companies Williams and Chevron are pivoting hard into building 'behind-the-meter' gas power plants dedicated to AI data centers — Williams for Meta in Ohio, Chevron for a 2.67-gigawatt Microsoft plant in Texas under a 20-year power purchase agreement — turning fossil fuel infrastructure into a structurally embedded, long-duration supplier to the AI buildout while emissions and grid-interconnection questions remain unresolved.

themes.theme: Fossil fuel pivot to AI data-center power

insights.claim: Williams and Chevron are presenting rising data-center demand for gas and power as a major growth driver to investors, following a banner year for oil and gas profits boosted by rising oil prices tied to conflict in the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Legacy oil and gas infrastructure companies are diversifying revenue into AI-driven power demand, creating a new investable linkage between fossil fuel capex cycles and the AI buildout — a hedge against long-term oil demand uncertainty.
insights.locator: But the artificial intelligence boom is also giving fossil fuel companies

insights.claim: BloombergNEF's global head of commodities and energy, Ashish Sethia, says data centers are becoming a major driver of both power and gas demand in the US, and a BloombergNEF report found the US would need to increase natural gas production by 36 percent by the mid-2030s, driven partly by data centers.
insights.speaker: Ashish Sethia (via Molly Taft)
insights.so_what: A 36% gas production increase forecast tied partly to data centers is a hard, quantified structural demand tailwind for US natural gas producers and midstream infrastructure companies through the mid-2030s.

insights.claim: Sethia observes that new data center announcements are increasingly clustering around areas that already have gas pipelines, and expects multiple companies beyond Williams and Chevron to benefit from building pipeline infrastructure for data centers.
insights.speaker: Ashish Sethia (via Molly Taft)
insights.so_what: Existing gas pipeline geography is becoming a siting determinant for AI data centers, meaning midstream pipeline owners with existing gas infrastructure footprints have a durable locational advantage in capturing future data-center power deals.
insights.locator: While Williams and Chevron are early movers

insights.claim: Williams, a major US oil and gas infrastructure company, is building six behind-the-meter (islanded, off-grid) gas power plants for data centers across the country, including four projects serving Meta data centers in Ohio, and in mid-July announced more than $5 billion in investment for its data-center ventures, including funding from private equity firm KKR.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A concrete $5B+ capital commitment with KKR participation signals institutional investor conviction in behind-the-meter gas-for-AI infrastructure as a distinct, financeable asset class separate from traditional utility-connected power.
insights.locator: In mid-July, Williams announced more than $5 billion

insights.claim: Williams' four Ohio power plants with filed permit applications could, per those applications, emit up to 9.6 million tons of greenhouse gases per year combined, equivalent to more than 22 average natural gas plants according to EPA figures, though a Williams spokesperson says actual emissions could be roughly two-thirds lower than permitted limits.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A large gap between permitted and claimed actual emissions is a recurring regulatory and reputational risk pattern investors should track, since permit ceilings — not company projections — are the enforceable legal exposure.
insights.locator: Williams' four power plants that have filed permit applications

insights.claim: Williams is building a 9-mile natural gas pipeline across an Ohio suburb, and company president Chad Zamarin said on a May earnings call that Williams deliberately 'overbuilt the capacity' of a pipeline serving one of its Meta-affiliated power plants so it could function as 'an energy artery along which other projects could be developed.'
insights.speaker: Chad Zamarin (via Molly Taft)
insights.so_what: Deliberately overbuilding pipeline capacity beyond a single customer's needs is a land-grab strategy to capture future regional data-center demand — a scalable, repeatable playbook other midstream operators may copy.
insights.quote: overbuilt the capacity ... be an energy artery along which other projects could be developed.
insights.locator: In an earnings call in May, Williams president Chad Zamarin

insights.claim: Williams' agreements with Meta for data center power run between 10 and 12.5 years, shorter than the 20-year agreement Chevron signed with Microsoft.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Contract duration is a useful comparative metric of counterparty commitment and revenue visibility across hyperscaler power deals; Chevron's longer Microsoft deal implies deeper capital-return certainty than Williams' Meta arrangements.
insights.locator: Williams' agreements with Meta for its data center power

insights.claim: Chevron is building a 2.67-gigawatt behind-the-meter gas power plant for a Microsoft data center in Texas, far larger than Williams' largest Meta plant (just under 700 megawatts), under a 20-year power purchase agreement that Chevron describes as the only 'multi-gigawatt' project with such a long-term contract in place.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A 2.67GW, 20-year contracted deal is an unusually large and long-duration commitment that locks in Chevron as a structural, multi-decade supplier to Microsoft's AI compute buildout — a scale benchmark for evaluating future oil-major/hyperscaler power deals.
insights.locator: the size of the 2.67-gigawatt project Chevron is building

insights.claim: Chevron reported its best quarterly profits in six years on the same Friday it highlighted the Microsoft data-center partnership across all of its investor materials.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Chevron is actively marketing its AI-data-center power business to investors alongside record profits, suggesting the company views this segment as a key forward growth narrative it wants priced into the stock.
insights.locator: The oil giant reported its best quarterly profits in six years

insights.claim: The Chevron-Microsoft power plant, according to its permit, could produce more than 11.5 million tons of carbon-dioxide-equivalent emissions per year — more than the combined 9.6 million tons across all four of Williams' Ohio plants.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A single Chevron-Microsoft facility's permitted emissions exceed Williams' entire four-plant Ohio buildout, underscoring the outsized climate footprint of the largest AI power deals and the associated regulatory/reputational exposure for Microsoft specifically.
insights.locator: The Chevron and Microsoft plant, according to its permit

insights.claim: Jeff Gustavson, president of Chevron's New Energies division, said on the company's earnings call that the Microsoft project 'provides a repeatable model' and that Chevron is already in talks with potential future data-center customers, adding that 'the grid cannot keep up with the demand from hyperscalers and others, and we see that persisting for years.'
insights.speaker: Jeff Gustavson (via Molly Taft)
insights.so_what: Chevron explicitly intends to replicate the Microsoft deal structure with additional hyperscaler customers, positioning its New Energies division as a recurring, scalable revenue line rather than a one-off project — a forward growth signal for Chevron's diversification thesis.
insights.quote: The grid cannot keep up with the demand from hyperscalers and others, and we see that persisting for years.
insights.locator: Jeff Gustavson, the president of Chevron's New Energies division

insights.claim: As WIRED reported previously, the Chevron-Microsoft power plant quietly applied for a school district tax break worth millions, which was finalized by the state late last month.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Public subsidy capture (tax breaks) alongside private power-purchase revenue improves the project's effective economics, a detail relevant to assessing the true return profile of large AI data-center energy deals.
insights.locator: the power plant quietly applied for a school district tax break

insights.claim: Whether these massive behind-the-meter plants will remain dedicated solely to data centers or eventually connect to the public grid is, according to BloombergNEF's Sethia, 'a massive question for the future of power prices in the country.'
insights.speaker: Ashish Sethia (via Molly Taft)
insights.so_what: The islanded-vs-grid-connected status of these mega-plants will materially affect regional electricity prices and grid capacity, making future interconnection filings and regulatory decisions a key catalyst to monitor for both AI infrastructure and utility investors.
insights.quote: a massive question for the future of power prices in the country
insights.locator: Whether these massive plants will stay serving data centers only

insights.claim: Chevron's investor materials indicate it expects to connect the Microsoft power plant to the grid sometime after 2030, and an interconnection application has already been submitted, even as Texas' grid faces significant interconnection delays; a Chevron spokesperson says future interconnection could enable export of surplus power and additional system redundancy.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A post-2030 grid-connection plan for a 2.67GW plant implies these facilities could eventually become significant new supply sources for Texas's ERCOT grid, but Texas's existing interconnection backlog is a real execution risk to that timeline.
insights.quote: Future interconnection could enable export of surplus power and provide additional system redundancy, if achieved.

insights.claim: Friends of the Earth deputy director Lukas Shankar-Ross argues that building large-scale fossil fuel infrastructure for data centers now is a 'lifeline' to an industry that needs to be phased out, and warns that if in 20 years there is a public grid dominated by renewables alongside a private grid dominated by fossil gas, Microsoft will bear some responsibility.
insights.speaker: Lukas Shankar-Ross (via Molly Taft)
insights.so_what: Presents the bear case: these long-duration gas contracts (10-20 years) risk locking hyperscalers into fossil infrastructure that outlasts near-term political cycles and could delay a broader renewable transition — a climate/ESG risk factor for Microsoft and Meta specifically.
insights.quote: If, 20 years from now, there's a public grid dominated by renewables, and a private grid dominated by fossil gas, Microsoft will bear some of the responsibility here.
insights.locator: Large gas plants are long-term investments

insights.claim: The Trump administration is actively encouraging tech companies to build their own power (behind-the-meter) rather than connect to the grid, amid rising utility bills that are fueling a national political backlash against data centers.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Federal policy is actively steering hyperscalers toward off-grid power specifically to avoid consumer electricity price impacts, which is a direct policy tailwind supporting the Williams/Chevron behind-the-meter business model.
insights.locator: With utility bills rising and helping to fuel the national backlash
